## Objectives

+ Forecast with **trend projection** — a regression of the series on the
  period number — and compute its MAD.
+ Test the residuals for **autocorrelation** with the **Durbin–Watson**
  statistic, and say what a positive result does to your regression.
+ Forecast with **multiplicative decomposition**: seasonal factors, a
  deseasonalised trend, and their product.
+ Represent seasonality with **dummy variables** in a multiple regression.
+ Choose among all of Chapter 16's methods for each challenge series, and
  defend the choice with a backtest.

::: {.charcoal}
You now have Chapters 14 and 15. That changes what you can do with a time
series: instead of averaging its past, you can *model* it — put the period
number on the right-hand side and let regression find the trend; put the
season on the right-hand side and let it find the calendar. The methods before
Exam 1 assumed a level. The methods before Exam 2 added a drifting level. These
add a trend and a season, which is everything in Donnelly's list of
components except the cycle.

The smoothing methods were atheoretic: they had nothing to say about *why* a
series moves. Regression is at least a hypothesis — sales grow with time;
March is bigger than February — and a hypothesis can be wrong in ways you can
check. That is the point of the Durbin–Watson test below.
:::

# Trend Projection

::: {.blue}
**Trend projection** fits a straight line to the series against the period
number and extends it into the future (Formula 16.6):

$$\hat{y}_t = b_0 + b_1 t,$$

with $b_1$ and $b_0$ the ordinary least-squares slope and intercept from
Chapter 14 (Formulas 16.7 and 16.8), $t = 1, 2, \ldots, n$.
:::

For Brandywine Ford, $t$ runs 1 to 12 and the regression is simple enough to
do by hand: $\sum t = 78$, $\sum y = 1{,}599$, $\sum ty = 10{,}783$,
$\sum t^2 = 650$.

```{python}
#| label: trend-fit
#| output: asis
y = CAR_SALES
tp = trend_projection(y, horizon=2)
show_math(r"\hat{y}_t = %.4f + %.4f\,t \qquad \hat{y}_{13} = %.4f + %.4f\,(13) = %.2f \approx %d \text{ cars}"
          % (tp["b0"], tp["b1"], tp["b0"], tp["b1"], tp["forecasts"].iloc[0],
             round(tp["forecasts"].iloc[0])))
```

Sales grow by about `{python} num(tp["b1"], 2)` cars a quarter. The forecast
for period 13 is `{python} num(tp["forecasts"].iloc[0], 0)`; for period 14 it
would be `{python} num(tp["forecasts"].iloc[1], 0)`, and each period further
out is a little less believable — a line extended is a line trusted.

```{python}
#| label: trend-table
tp["table"].round(1)
```

The forecasting error of a regression is its **residual**, $e_t = y_t -
\hat{y}_t$ (Formula 16.9), and the MAD is the mean absolute residual:
`{python} num(tp["MAD"])` cars. Note that this MAD averages all twelve
residuals — regression forecasts every period, including the first.

```{python}
#| label: trend-excel
pd.DataFrame({"coef": [tp["b0"], tp["b1"]], "std error": tp["se"], "t": tp["t"],
              "p-value": tp["p"]}, index=["Intercept", "Period"]).round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: trend-r2
#| include: false
r2, adj, se = tp["r2"], tp["adj_r2"], tp["std_error"]
```

This is what Excel's Regression tool prints (Figure 16.11C): $R^2 =$
`{python} num(r2, 4)`, standard error `{python} num(se, 2)`, and a p-value
of `{python} num(tp["p"][1], 4)` on the slope. At $\alpha = 0.05$ the trend
is *not* statistically significant — and yet its MAD is among the best so
far. Those are different questions. Significance asks whether the slope could
be zero given twelve noisy quarters; the MAD asks how far off the forecasts
were. A line can forecast usefully without proving anything.

```{python}
#| label: trend-plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.4))
t = np.arange(1, 13)
ax.scatter(t, y.values, color=UNLV_SCARLET, zorder=5, label="actual")
ax.plot(t, tp["table"]["fitted"], color=UNLV_GRAY, linewidth=1.4, label="trend line")
tf = np.array([13, 14])
ax.plot(np.r_[12, tf], np.r_[tp["table"]["fitted"].iloc[-1], tp["forecasts"].values],
        color=UNLV_GRAY, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.4, label="projection")
ax.scatter(tf, tp["forecasts"].values, color=UNLV_GRAY, zorder=5)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(1, 15)); ax.set_xlabel("Period"); ax.set_ylabel("Cars sold")
ax.set_title("Figure 16.9: forecasting with a trend projection", color=UNLV_SCARLET)
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6"); ax.legend(frameon=False)
for side in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

# Checking for Autocorrelation

Regression assumes the residuals are independent of one another. In a time
series that assumption fails more often than it holds, because whatever
pushed this quarter's sales above the line is usually still pushing next
quarter.

::: {.blue}
**Autocorrelation** is the condition in which the residuals of a regression
are not independent of one another. The **Durbin–Watson statistic** tests for
it (Formula 16.10):

$$d = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^{n}(e_t - e_{t-1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} e_t^2}.$$

$d$ ranges from 0 to 4. A value near 2 means no autocorrelation; near 0,
perfect positive autocorrelation (residuals in long runs of the same sign);
near 4, perfect negative autocorrelation (residuals that alternate).
:::

If consecutive residuals are close to each other, the numerator is small and
$d$ falls toward zero. Donnelly's Table 16.10 makes the point with five
residuals all equal to 20: every difference is zero, $d = 0$, and knowing
one residual tells you the next exactly. Negative autocorrelation is rare in
business data, so the test is one-tailed:

$$H_0: \text{no positive autocorrelation} \qquad H_1: \text{positive autocorrelation is present}.$$

The test needs at least 15 observations, so the book switches to a 16-year
series of union membership as a share of the labour force (Table 16.12):

```{python}
#| label: union
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.4f}")
union = pd.Series([13.0, 12.6, 12.5, 12.1, 12.2, 12.5, 12.4, 12.5,
                   11.9, 11.8, 11.3, 11.3, 11.1, 11.1, 10.7, 10.7],
                  index=range(2002, 2018), name="pct_union")
u = trend_projection(union)
res = u["table"]["residual"]
pieces = pd.DataFrame({"residual": res, "prior": res.shift(1),
                       "(e_t - e_t-1)^2": (res - res.shift(1)) ** 2, "e_t^2": res ** 2})
pieces.round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: dw-math
#| output: asis
dwr = dw_test(res)
show_math(r"\hat{y}_t = %.4f %+.4f\,t \qquad d = \frac{%.4f}{%.4f} = %.4f"
          % (u["b0"], u["b1"], pieces["(e_t - e_t-1)^2"].sum(), pieces["e_t^2"].sum(), dwr["d"]))
```

The critical values come from the Durbin–Watson table (Appendix A, Table 9),
indexed by $n$ and by $k$, the number of independent variables. For $n = 16$,
$k = 1$, $\alpha = 0.05$: $d_L$ = `{python} str(dwr["d_L"])` and
$d_U$ = `{python} str(dwr["d_U"])`. The decision rule has three regions:

| Result | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| $d < d_L$ | Reject $H_0$: positive autocorrelation is present |
| $d_L \le d \le d_U$ | Inconclusive |
| $d > d_U$ | Fail to reject $H_0$: no evidence of positive autocorrelation |

Here $d$ = `{python} num(dwr["d"], 3)` $< d_L$, so we **`{python} dwr["verdict"]`**.
(The book gets 1.0085 from residuals rounded to three decimals; the
difference is rounding, not disagreement.)

::: {.charcoal}
What does a positive result cost you? The point estimates $b_0$ and $b_1$ are
still unbiased; the *standard errors* are wrong, usually too small, so the
t-test on the slope claims more certainty than it has. The trend line may
still forecast tolerably. But autocorrelated residuals are also a message:
there is information in the residuals a better model could use. If the last
three residuals were negative, the next one probably is too — and the trend
projection ignores that, while the naive forecast, without knowing it, uses
it. The fix Donnelly suggests is to add an explanatory variable. Another,
which you will meet if you take a time-series course, is to model the
residuals themselves.
:::

# Forecasting with Seasonality

Look at the car sales again: quarters 2 and 4 spike, every year. Every method
so far has treated that as noise. It is not noise; it is the calendar, and a
calendar can be forecast.

## Multiplicative Decomposition

::: {.blue}
The **multiplicative decomposition** model writes each observation as the
product of its components (Formula 16.11):

$$y_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_t,$$

trend, seasonal and random. (The cycle is left out: three years of data are
not enough to see one.) The forecast is $F_t = T_t \times S_t$ (Formula
16.14) — the random component is, by definition, unforecastable.
:::

Four steps: identify the seasonal factors, deseasonalise the data, fit a trend
to the deseasonalised data, and multiply.

### Step 1: the centered moving average

Average four consecutive quarters. Because four is even, the average of
periods 1–4 belongs to period 2.5, halfway between 2 and 3; so average the
period-2.5 and period-3.5 averages to get a value centred *on* period 3. That
is the **centered moving average**, and it contains one of every season, so
the seasonal component has been averaged out of it — and so, roughly, has the
random component. What is left is the trend: $\text{CMA}_t \approx T_t$.

### Step 2: the ratio to moving average

Divide each actual by its CMA (Formula 16.12): $\text{RMA}_t = y_t /
\text{CMA}_t = S_t \times R_t$. The ratio is what the season and the noise
did to that period.

```{python}
#| label: decomp-steps
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.4f}")
dec = decompose(y, season_length=4, horizon=4)
dec["steps"].round(4)
```

Read period 3: CMA `{python} num(dec["steps"].loc["2016Q3", "CMA"], 3)`, actual
108, ratio `{python} num(dec["steps"].loc["2016Q3", "RMA"], 4)` — the third
quarter of 2016 ran about 12% below trend. The first two and last two periods
have no CMA: a centred average needs data on both sides.

### Step 3: seasonal factors, then normalise them

Each quarter appears twice in the ratios. Average them, and the random
component — which is what differs between the two years — cancels, leaving
the seasonal factor. Then rescale so the four factors sum to exactly 4,
because a "season" that averages more than 100% of an average quarter is not
a season.

```{python}
#| label: decomp-factors
dec["factors"].round(4)
```

The sum of the raw factors is `{python} num(dec["factors"].attrs["sum_SF"], 4)`;
multiplying each by 4 / `{python} num(dec["factors"].attrs["sum_SF"], 4)`
gives the normalised factors. Quarter 2 runs about
`{python} num((dec["factors"].loc[2, "NSF"] - 1) * 100, 0)`% above an
average quarter; quarters 1 and 3 run about 10% below.

### Step 4: deseasonalise, fit the trend, multiply

Divide each observation by its quarter's factor (Formula 16.13) and the
seasonal spikes disappear. Regress what is left on the period number; that is
the trend component. The forecast is the projected trend times the factor for
the quarter being forecast.

```{python}
#| label: decomp-table
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}")
dec["table"].round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: decomp-math
#| output: asis
f13 = dec["future"].iloc[0]
show_math(r"T_t = %.4f + %.4f\,t \qquad T_{13} = %.2f \qquad F_{13} = T_{13} \times S_1 = %.2f \times %.4f = %.1f \approx %d \text{ cars}"
          % (dec["b0"], dec["b1"], f13["T"], f13["T"], f13["S"], f13["forecast"], round(f13["forecast"])))
```

```{python}
#| label: decomp-future
dec["future"].round(2)
```

The trend alone would have said `{python} num(f13["T"], 0)` cars; the first
quarter's factor pulls it down to `{python} num(f13["forecast"], 0)`. And the
MAD is `{python} num(dec["MAD"])` — less than half of any method before it.
(The book's trend line, $116.85 + 2.52t$, was fitted to deseasonalised
values rounded to one decimal; ours is fitted to the unrounded ones.)

```{python}
#| label: decomp-plot
_ = forecast_plot(y, {"decomposition": dec["forecast"], "SMA p=4": sma_forecast(y, 4)},
                  title="Multiplicative decomposition follows the season; the average smooths it away",
                  ylab="Cars sold")
```

## Seasonality with Dummy Variables

Chapter 15 gave you dummy variables. A season is a qualitative variable with
four categories, so it needs three dummies (one category is the base):

::: {.blue}
$$F_t = b_0 + b_1 t + b_2\,\text{SD}_2 + b_3\,\text{SD}_3 + b_4\,\text{SD}_4,$$

where $\text{SD}_q = 1$ in quarter $q$ and 0 otherwise, and the first quarter
is the base. Each $b_q$ is how many more cars quarter $q$ sells than the
first quarter *at the same point on the trend*.
:::

The book runs best-subsets regression and keeps the period and two of the
three dummies — the third-quarter dummy is dropped, because the third quarter
is not distinguishable from the first. Dummies are named here by quarter, so
the book's SD$_1$ and SD$_3$ are our SD$_2$ and SD$_4$.

```{python}
#| label: dummies
book = seasonal_dummy_regression(y, season_length=4, base_season=1, horizon=4, drop=[3])
book["coef"].round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: dummies-stats
#| include: false
b = book["coef"]["coef"]
```

Adjusted $R^2$ is `{python} num(book["adj_r2"], 3)` and every coefficient has
$p < 0.05$. The second quarter sells `{python} num(b["SD2"])` more cars than
the first; the fourth, `{python} num(b["SD4"])` more. That is the
decomposition's seasonal factor of `{python} num(dec["factors"].loc[2, "NSF"], 2)`
said in cars rather than ratios.

```{python}
#| label: dummies-math
#| output: asis
show_math(r"F_{13} = %.4f + %.1f\,(13) + %.4f\,(0) + %.4f\,(0) = %.1f \approx %d \text{ cars}"
          % (b["intercept"], b["t"], b["SD2"], b["SD4"], book["future"]["forecast"].iloc[0],
             round(book["future"]["forecast"].iloc[0])))
```

```{python}
#| label: dummies-future
book["future"].round(1)
```

## Table 16.22: every method, one table

```{python}
#| label: everything
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.2f}")
accuracy(y, {
    "naive":                            naive_forecast(y),
    "SMA p=3":                          sma_forecast(y, 3),
    "SMA p=4":                          sma_forecast(y, 4),
    "WMA 3-2-1":                        wma_forecast(y, [1, 2, 3]),
    "Exp. smoothing 0.6":               exp_smooth(y, 0.6),
    "Exp. smoothing w/ trend 0.3, 0.1": exp_smooth_trend(y, 0.3, 0.1),
    "Trend projection":                 tp["forecast"],
    "Multiplicative decomposition":     dec["forecast"],
    "Seasonal dummies":                 book["forecast"],
}).round(2)
```

::: {.charcoal}
The two methods that model *both* trend and season win by a wide margin, and
the four-period moving average — the only smoothing method whose window spans
every season — is next. Complexity is not what wins. Matching the method to
the components that are actually in the series is what wins, and a method
that models a component the series does not have loses ground for it. The
next section shows both halves of that.
:::

# The Challenge Series

## Las Vegas visitor volume: twelve seasons

Visitor volume is monthly, so there are twelve seasons, and the LVCVA does
not seasonally adjust it. This is the challenge series with the strongest
calendar in it.

```{python}
#| label: lv-plot
_ = time_series(lv.index.to_timestamp(), lv.values,
                title="Las Vegas visitor volume, monthly (LVCVA)", ylab="Visitors")
```

::: {.scarlet}
2020 and 2021 are not a season; they are a pandemic. A seasonal factor for
April averaged across a closed city and an open one describes neither. Every
seasonal model below starts in January 2022. That is a judgment, and it is
the kind of judgment the data cannot make for you.
:::

```{python}
#| label: lv-decomp
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}")
post = lv.loc["2022-01":]
month_of = post.index.month
d12 = decompose(post, season_length=12, horizon=3, season_of=month_of)
d12["factors"]["NSF"].round(3).to_frame("NSF").T
```

```{python}
#| label: lv-facts
#| include: false
nsf = d12["factors"]["NSF"]
hi_m, lo_m = int(nsf.idxmax()), int(nsf.idxmin())
import calendar
hi_name, lo_name = calendar.month_name[hi_m], calendar.month_name[lo_m]
next_p = post.index[-1] + 1
```

The factors say `{python} hi_name` runs about
`{python} num((nsf.max() - 1) * 100, 0)`% above an average month and
`{python} lo_name` about `{python} num((1 - nsf.min()) * 100, 0)`% below.
The deseasonalised trend is `{python} num(d12["b0"], 0)`
`{python} "+" if d12["b1"] >= 0 else "−"` `{python} num(abs(d12["b1"]), 0)`
visitors per month — read the sign; it is the post-2022 direction of the
market, and it is what the seasonal factor gets multiplied by.

```{python}
#| label: lv-future
fut = d12["future"].copy()
fut["T"] = fut["T"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}")
fut["forecast"] = fut["forecast"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}")
fut
```

```{python}
#| label: lv-dummies
sd12 = seasonal_dummy_regression(post, season_length=12, base_season=1, horizon=3,
                                 season_of=month_of)
sd12["future"].assign(forecast=lambda d: d["forecast"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}"))
```

```{python}
#| label: lv-accuracy
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}")
lv_methods = {
    "naive":            naive_forecast(post),
    "SMA p=3":          sma_forecast(post, 3),
    "SMA p=12":         sma_forecast(post, 12),
    "ES 0.3":           exp_smooth(post, 0.3),
    "Trend projection": trend_projection(post)["forecast"],
    "Decomposition":    d12["forecast"],
    "Seasonal dummies": sd12["forecast"],
}
accuracy(post, lv_methods).round(0)
```

```{python}
#| label: lv-backtest
btl = backtest_summary(post, {
    "naive":    (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=12": (sma_forecast, {"p": 12}),
    "ES 0.3":   (exp_smooth, {"alpha": 0.3}),
    "Decomposition": (lambda s: decompose(s, 12, season_of=s.index.month)["forecast"], {}),
    "Seasonal dummies": (lambda s: seasonal_dummy_regression(
        s, 12, season_of=s.index.month)["forecast"], {}),
}, last=12)
btl.round(0)
```

```{python}
#| label: lv-dw
#| include: false
dw_lv = dw_test(sd12["table"]["residual"])
```

Backtested over the last twelve months, the best method for
`{python} str(next_p)` is **`{python} btl["MAD"].idxmin()`**, and the naive
forecast — which knows nothing about calendars — is at
`{python} num(btl.loc["naive", "MAD"], 0)`. The twelve-month moving average
does respectably for the same reason the four-quarter average did on car
sales: its window contains every season once.

One more thing to check, now that you know how. The Durbin–Watson statistic
on the dummy model's residuals is `{python} num(dw_lv["d"], 3)` against
$d_L$ = `{python} str(dw_lv["d_L"])`: **`{python} dw_lv["verdict"]`**. The
residuals run in streaks — a slow spring is followed by a slow summer — and
the seasonal model cannot see that. That is exactly the situation in which a
forecast that blends the model with the latest residual will beat the model
alone, and it is the next thing you would learn in a forecasting course.

```{python}
#| label: lv-forecast-plot
_ = forecast_plot(post, {"seasonal dummies": sd12["forecast"], "naive": naive_forecast(post)},
                  title="Las Vegas visitor volume: actual vs. forecast", ylab="Visitors", last=30)
```

## Nevada house prices: a very significant line that keeps missing

```{python}
#| label: hpi-trend
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}")
recent = hpi.loc["2015Q1":]
th = trend_projection(recent, horizon=2)
dw_h = dw_test(th["table"]["residual"])
th["table"]["residual"].tail(8).round(2).to_frame("residual").T
```

`{python} str(len(recent))` quarters from 2015, and the trend line is $T_t$ = `{python} num(th["b0"], 1)` + `{python} num(th["b1"], 2)` $t$
with $R^2$ = `{python} num(th["r2"], 3)` and a slope p-value of `{python} f"{th['p'][1]:.1e}"`. The forecast for `{python} str(recent.index[-1] + 1)`
is `{python} num(th["forecasts"].iloc[0])`; the naive forecast is
`{python} num(recent.iloc[-1])`. The Durbin–Watson statistic is
`{python} num(dw_h["d"], 3)`: **`{python} dw_h["verdict"]`**.

Look at the last eight residuals in the table above: residuals that keep the
same sign for quarters at a time are what a small $d$ looks like. The line is
straight and the index is not: it rose fast, then slowed, and a line fitted
through both halves misses the recent quarters in the same direction every
time. A regression can be overwhelmingly significant and still be the wrong
shape. The naive forecast, which knows only where the index *is*, has the
last residual built in; the trend-adjusted smoothing from Part 2 tracks the
slope as it changes. Check both against the line in your backtest before you
submit a trend projection for this series.

## Housing starts: read the units line first

```{python}
#| label: houst-factors
h_recent = houst.loc["2019-01":]
hd = decompose(h_recent, season_length=12, season_of=h_recent.index.month)
hd["factors"]["NSF"].round(3).to_frame("NSF").T
```

FRED's units line for HOUST reads *Thousands of Units, Seasonally Adjusted
Annual Rate*. The Census Bureau removed the season before FRED published the
number, and the factors a decomposition finds anyway range only
`{python} num(hd["factors"]["NSF"].min(), 3)` to
`{python} num(hd["factors"]["NSF"].max(), 3)`. A seasonal model here is
fitting noise, and it will cost you accuracy for the privilege. The same is
true of the CPI and of initial claims (both SA); it is **not** true of the
Nevada house price index (NSA) or of visitor volume.

```{python}
#| label: houst-backtest
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}")
backtest_summary(h_recent, {
    "naive":   (naive_forecast, {}),
    "SMA p=3": (sma_forecast, {"p": 3}),
    "SMA p=6": (sma_forecast, {"p": 6}),
    "ES 0.3":  (exp_smooth, {"alpha": 0.3}),
    "Trend":   (lambda s: trend_projection(s)["forecast"], {}),
}, last=12).round(1)
```

::: {.charcoal}
**The map of the challenge, after three notes.** Each series has a method
that suits it, and the reasons are the components in Donnelly's list. The CPI:
trend, no season → trend-adjusted smoothing. Initial claims: noise around a
level → a short moving average or exponential smoothing with a moderate
$\alpha$. Housing starts: already seasonally adjusted, noisy → a short moving
average. The Nevada HPI: a trend that bends → smoothing that tracks the slope,
not a fixed line. Visitor volume: a strong calendar → decomposition or
dummies, refit as the months arrive. Whether that map is still right next
month is what the backtest is for.
:::

## Verify

| Check | What it catches |
|---|---|
| The seasonal factors sum to the number of seasons | Unnormalised factors, which bias every forecast the same direction |
| The first and last CMA rows are blank | A "centred" average that is not centred |
| The dummy for the base season is absent | A model with $k$ dummies for $k$ seasons, which will not estimate |
| The forecast's season matches the calendar month being forecast | A factor applied to the wrong month — the commonest error in this section |
| The units line was read before a seasonal model was fitted | A season fitted to a seasonally adjusted series |
| $n \ge 15$ before a Durbin–Watson verdict is reported | A test the table cannot support |

# Your Turn (from the textbook)

Using the GPA series (three seasons a year: Fall, Spring, Summer): find the
seasonal factors (Your Turn 7), forecast the next three semesters by
multiplicative decomposition (Your Turn 8), and compute its MAD (Your Turn
9). Three seasons is odd, so the moving average is already centred and there
is no second averaging step — check that the code agrees.

```{python}
#| label: gpa-answer
#| code-fold: true
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.3f}")
gpa = pd.Series([2.5, 2.2, 2.7, 3.0, 2.6, 3.0, 3.2, 2.7, 3.3],
                index=["Fr Fall", "Fr Spring", "Fr Summer", "So Fall", "So Spring",
                       "So Summer", "Jr Fall", "Jr Spring", "Jr Summer"], name="GPA")
g = decompose(gpa, season_length=3, horizon=3)
print(g["factors"].round(4))
print(g["future"].round(3))
print(f"MAD: {g['MAD']:.3f}")
```
